source_read: PMC HTML full text PMC6497989 (Lancet version), all sections including the panel, the Research in context box, Tables 1 and 2 as text, acknowledgments and declaration of interests. Figures 2-5 are images; their printed values (category intakes, slopes, case numbers) were read on the PMC figure pages in my own tab, and the non-drinker and ex-drinker points of Figures 4 and 5 were only read approximately, since they are plotted without numbers. The supplementary appendix (PDF) and the linked comment and letter were not read.

claims.overstatement: Wording. The headline pairs Chinese men with 'more high blood pressure (hypertension)', but this source reports mean systolic pressure only, with no hypertension outcome, so that part rests on the European studies; the sentence should make this clear. Also, '161,498 genotyped Chinese adults' is the whole genotyped set; the genetic systolic estimate comes from 55 879 men (Table 2; 55 897 in Figure 3D).
claims.note: Numbers check. Genetic +4.3 mm Hg (3.7 to 4.9) and conventional +4.8 (4.5 to 5.1) per 280 g/week; women -0.6 (-1.0 to -0.1). Recomputed: 280 g/week / 7 = 40 g/day; 4.3 x 100/280 = 1.54, so 'about 1.5 mm Hg per 100 g a week' is right, given the linearity assumption the claim states. Comparison groups: the genetic slope runs across six genotype-area categories (men's mean intake 4 to 256 g/week), stratified by area and adjusted for age; the conventional slope is among current drinkers, against usual intake (corrected for regression dilution), adjusted for age, area, education, income and smoking. The authors warn that under-reported intake would make all slopes too steep.

anchors.locator: Results, 6th paragraph; Figure 3, panels A and D
anchors.extracted: Men: systolic +4.8 mm Hg (95% CI 4.5 to 5.1) per 280 g/week usual intake among current drinkers (conventional; panel A n 193 003); +4.3 (3.7 to 4.9) per 280 g/week genotype-predicted mean male intake (genetic; panel D n 55 897); current drinkers' mean intake about 280 g/week; both P<0.0001.

Men (n 55 879), categories 1-6: 129.7, 130.0, 130.5, 131.6, 133.0, 134.1 mm Hg; slope 4.3 (3.7 to 4.9). Women (n 83 017): 129.7 to 128.5; slope -0.6 (-1.0 to -0.1) per 280 g/week of men's mean intake; men's effect larger than women's, P<0.0001.
Men's mean weekly intake by category 4, 18, 34, 78, 130, 256 g, ever drinking in most weeks 3% to 74%; women under 2 to 8 g a week, under 1% to 6%.

Both approaches indicate about 5 mm Hg higher systolic pressure per 280 g/week; the authors link this, from conventional data in the same cohort, to about 15% more ischaemic heart disease and ischaemic stroke and about 30% more intracerebral haemorrhage.

Intake is self-reported and may be under-reported; if true intake was higher, all conventional and genetic slopes are too steep; genetic slopes would be about 10% steeper if ex-drinkers had been counted as zero intake.

claims.note: Supported for the Chinese men: the conventional analyses show lower heart-attack and coronary rates at moderate intake (about 100 g/week, one to two drinks a day in the authors' terms) than in non-drinkers and ex-drinkers. Comparison groups: the reference is the lowest-intake current drinkers (under 140 g/week). Non-drinkers here are people who drank nothing in the past year and never drank weekly, so ex-drinkers and occasional drinkers are counted separately. Their relative risks are plotted but not printed (roughly 1.6 for heart attack and 1.3 for coronary heart disease, read from the plots), so the claim's 'no values printed' is right. Participants with previous coronary heart disease, stroke or transient ischaemic attack were excluded.

anchors.locator: Results, 10th paragraph; Figure 5, panels A and B
anchors.extracted: Conventional, men: U-shaped associations; moderate intake had substantially lower acute myocardial infarction (2958 cases) and total coronary (14 326) rates than non-drinkers or ex-drinkers, persisting in sensitivity analyses (appendix). Among current drinkers, RR per 280 g/week 1.15 (0.96 to 1.38) and 1.12 (1.04 to 1.21). Non-drinker values plotted only.

anchors.locator: Methods › Alcohol drinking patterns; Methods › Statistical analysis, 1st paragraph; Figure 5 legend
anchors.extracted: Groups: current (weekly in the past year), non-drinkers (none in the past year, never weekly), occasional, ex-drinkers. Conventional reference: current drinkers with the lowest intake. People with prior coronary disease, stroke or TIA excluded from incidence analyses.

claims.overstatement: Mild. 'Were not associated with heart attack' needs the authors' caveat: myocardial infarction cases were limited, and they say some real benefit or hazard cannot be excluded (0.96, 0.78 to 1.18 per 280 g/week). As written, it can read as evidence of no effect.
claims.note: Numbers check: myocardial infarction 0.96 (0.78 to 1.18; P=0.69; 1696 cases), coronary heart disease 1.05 (0.94 to 1.17; P=0.40; 6145 cases, Figure 5D), group means 4 to 256 g/week, 280 g/week = 40 g/day, rs671 GG v AG 1.02 (0.92 to 1.13), rs1229984 1.11 (0.95 to 1.31), women 0.94 (0.74 to 1.20). Instrument strength: men's mean intake was 3, 37 and 157 g/week by rs671 genotype and 98, 106 and 157 g/week by rs1229984 genotype; no F statistic. Checks for other pathways: women were used as a negative control (no adverse associations; slightly lower blood pressure; small differences in height, waist and hip); adjusting for education, income and smoking did not change the results; categories did not differ much in smoking; the authors note that both enzymes act in many pathways. Previous east Asian meta-analyses (second-hand) linked the alcohol-tolerant rs671 allele with lower coronary risk; this study does not support them.

anchors.locator: Results, 11th paragraph; Figure 5, panels C and D
anchors.extracted: Genetic, men: RR per 280 g/week genotype-predicted mean intake 0.96 (0.78 to 1.18; P=0.69; 1696 cases) for acute myocardial infarction, 1.05 (0.94 to 1.17; P=0.40; 6145 cases) for total coronary heart disease.

anchors.locator: Table 2, acute myocardial infarction columns; Results, 13th paragraph
anchors.extracted: Women 0.94 (0.74 to 1.20; 1246 events); P=0.45 for a larger effect in men. Single variants in men, GG v AG: rs671 1.02 (0.92 to 1.13), rs1229984 1.11 (0.95 to 1.31) for myocardial infarction.

Genetic heart-disease results are harder to interpret; little net effect from near zero to about 250 g/week; cases limited, so real benefit or hazard cannot be excluded; rs671 result does not support earlier east Asian meta-analyses.

Men's mean intake by rs671 AA/AG/GG 3, 37, 157 g/week (current drinkers 1%, 16%, 45%); by rs1229984 98, 106, 157 (32%, 33%, 43%); category means 4 to 256 g/week; no large genotype-related differences in smoking or other baseline traits (appendix).

anchors.locator: Results, 12th paragraph; Methods › Statistical analysis, 3rd and 4th paragraphs; Discussion, 13th paragraph
anchors.extracted: Genetic analyses stratified by area, adjusted for age; adding education, income and smoking did not change results. Women as a pleiotropy check: no adverse associations, slight favourable blood-pressure difference, small anthropometric effects; both enzymes act in many pathways.
Same men, self-reported drinking: moderate intake had substantially lower heart-attack rates than non-drinkers or ex-drinkers.

claims.note: Numbers check: per 280 g/week 1.27 (1.13 to 1.43), 1.58 (1.36 to 1.84) and 1.38 (1.26 to 1.51), with 5709, 2790 and 9189 cases (Figure 4D-F); per 100 g/week 1.09, 1.18 and 1.12; single variants 1.19 and 1.19; women 0.98 and 0.96; conventional 1.28, 1.59 and 1.35 (Figure 4C). Recomputed: 1.27^(100/280) = 1.09, 1.58^(100/280) = 1.18, 1.38^(100/280) = 1.12; 100/7 = 14.3 g/day. The attributable fractions are consistent with one third of men drinking about 280 g/week: 0.333 x 0.27 / (1 + 0.333 x 0.27) = 8.3%, and the same with 0.58 gives 16.2%. Table 2 category relative risks (ischaemic stroke 1.00, 1.00, 1.03, 1.11, 1.23, 1.23; intracerebral haemorrhage 1.00, 1.01, 1.02, 1.08, 1.29, 1.54) support 'the next two groups had higher risk'; the pooled comparison itself is in the appendix (p 26). The claim keeps the authors' condition (no protective effect, log-linear relation), which the paper's own Research in context box leaves out. Design point: the 161 498 genotyped include 10 470 people selected because they had a stroke or coronary event; how they were handled is in the appendix.

anchors.extracted: Genetic, men, per 280 g/week genotype-predicted mean intake: ischaemic stroke 1.27 (1.13 to 1.43; 5709 cases), intracerebral haemorrhage 1.58 (1.36 to 1.84; 2790), total 1.38 (1.26 to 1.51; 9189); IS v ICH P=0.01. Per 100 g/week 1.09 (1.04 to 1.14), 1.18 (1.12 to 1.24), 1.12 (1.09 to 1.16); range 4 to 256 g/week.

No raised risk in category 1 (two-thirds non-drinkers); no material departure from log-linearity; categories 4-5 (about 100 g/week) against pooled 1-3 (about 25 g/week) still adverse for ischaemic stroke and ICH (appendix p 26); directionally consistent in each area.

anchors.locator: Table 2, ischaemic stroke and intracerebral haemorrhage columns
anchors.extracted: Men's category RRs, ischaemic stroke 1.00, 1.00, 1.03, 1.11, 1.23, 1.23; ICH 1.00, 1.01, 1.02, 1.08, 1.29, 1.54. Women, per 280 g/week of men's intake: 0.98 (0.88 to 1.09; 7087 events) and 0.96 (0.82 to 1.12; 2525); men larger P=0.0007 and <0.0001.

Conventional, men: U-shape; about 100 g/week had lower stroke risk than non-drinkers and especially ex-drinkers (plotted only). Current drinkers per 280 g/week: IS 1.28 (1.19 to 1.38), ICH 1.59 (1.37 to 1.85), total 1.35 (1.27 to 1.44); 14 930, 3496, 19 859 cases; U-shape persisted in sensitivity analyses.
Single variants in men, GG v AG: stroke 1.19 (1.13 to 1.24) for rs671 and 1.19 (1.11 to 1.27) for rs1229984; neither variant associated with stroke in women.

Only if there is no material protective effect and the relation is about log-linear: excess risks 27% and 58% per 280 g/week (about the mean of the one-third of men who drank) imply alcohol was responsible for about 8% of ischaemic strokes and 16% of ICH among all men.

anchors.locator: Methods › Study design and participants, 1st paragraph; Methods › Genotyping and biochemistry, 1st paragraph; Results, 1st paragraph
anchors.extracted: 512 715 adults, ten areas, 28% of invitees; about 10 years' follow-up, 0.9% lost. 161 498 genotyped: 151 028 at random plus 10 470 chosen because they had a stroke or coronary event (used only in disease analyses).

key_findings.note: Case numbers 2958 and 14 326 are printed in Figure 5A-B, not in the text.
The source says alcohol 'was responsible for' these shares; the condition is attached in the Discussion, 7th paragraph.

reporting_issues.note: Found independently: Table 2 heading says 55 879 and Figure 3D says 55 897.

risk_of_bias.note: Some concerns overall; the domain notes match the source, including the 10 470 case-selected participants whose handling is described only in the appendix.

interpretation_gap.note: Minor for the main Interpretation. It should also note that the Research in context box (Implications) gives the 8% and 16% attributable shares without the condition the Discussion attaches (see missed).

missed: Research in context › Implications of all the available evidence: the attributable shares (about 8% of ischaemic strokes and 16% of intracerebral haemorrhages in men) are stated without the condition given in the Discussion, 7th paragraph (no material protective effect and a roughly log-linear relation). This is a reporting issue: claims must keep the condition.
Results, 9th paragraph: blood-pressure and stroke slopes looked steeper in men under 60 at baseline, but the authors say the numbers were too small for this to be reliable (appendix p 30).

Discussion, 4th paragraph: about 5 mm Hg per 280 g/week, in both analyses, corresponds in conventional data from this cohort to about 15% more ischaemic heart disease and ischaemic stroke and about 30% more intracerebral haemorrhage; the excess stroke risk seen genetically is about twice that (Discussion, 8th paragraph, which the card does record).
